## Overview

Before the optimum moves, each population in the paper spends 10,000 generations under
stabilising selection, so that it starts the experiment at equilibrium. How much genetic
variance it holds then matters: the genetic variance $V_G$ is the raw material of the
response to a moving optimum. This vignette measures the equilibrium and compares it
with two classical approximations.

Mutation adds variance and stabilising selection and drift remove it. Write $V_m$ for
the variance mutation adds per generation, $V_s = \omega^2 + V_E$ for the width of
selection on genotypes (the fitness function, widened by environmental noise), $n$ for
the number of loci, $\mu$ for the mutation rate per locus, $\alpha^2$ for the variance
of a mutation's effect and $N_e$ for the effective population size.

- Lande's Gaussian approximation [@Lande1975] assumes many alleles of small effect:
  $V_G \approx \sqrt{V_m V_s}$.
- The stochastic house-of-cards approximation [@Burger1989] allows for rare mutations
  of large effect and for drift:
  $V_G \approx 4 n \mu V_s \,/\, \left(1 + V_s / (N_e \alpha^2)\right)$.
  This is the approximation the paper compares its simulations with (its Supplementary
  Figure S1, labelled equation 21a in its results table).

## Setup

```{julia}
using QTLSim
using CairoMakie, Distributions, Printf, Random, Statistics
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
Threads.nthreads()
```

## The mutational input

Each offspring chromosome receives a Poisson number of mutations with mean
$n\mu$, and each mutation adds a Gaussian effect of variance
$\alpha^2 = m V_E / (2 n \mu)$ to a random locus. The scaling is chosen so that, in
expectation, mutation adds exactly $V_m = m V_E$ to the genetic variance of a diploid
individual each generation, whatever the number of loci and the mutation rate. That
statement is proved in Lean (`mutationalVarianceInput_eq` in
`lean/CategoricalQuantGen/Mutation.lean`); here we check it by applying the mutation
operator to a large population of zero genomes, for several locus counts and rates.

```{julia}
function mutational_input(p; rounds = 20, seed = 1)
    w = World(p); rng = Xoshiro(seed); Δ = Float64[]
    for _ in 1:rounds
        setgenomes!(w, zeros(p.NoQTL, p.Ploidy, p.PopSize); offspring = true)
        mutate!(w, rng)                       # adds mutations to the offspring buffer
        G = genomes(w; offspring = true)
        append!(Δ, sum(@view G[:, :, j]) for j in 1:p.PopSize)
    end
    var(Δ)
end

for (k, (L, rate)) in enumerate(((10, 1e-3), (100, 1e-4), (100, 1e-2), (1000, 1e-3)))
    p = Params(PopSize = 20_000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = L, MutationRatePerGamete = rate,
               PhenotypeVar = 0.02, Heritability = 0.4, MutationScalar = 0.004)
    @printf("NoQTL = %4d, rate = %.0e (%4.2f mutations per gamete):  variance added %.3e   (m·V_E = %.3e)\n",
            L, rate, L * rate, mutational_input(p; seed = k), muteVar(p))
end
```

The input agrees with $m V_E$ to within sampling error in every case, even though the
number of mutations per generation differs a hundred-fold between the rows.

## Where the "analytical" fitness width comes from

When `InitFitnessSD` is not given, QTSim and this package use
$\omega = V_G / \sqrt{m V_E}$ with $V_G = h^2 V_P$. That is the Gaussian approximation
solved for $\omega$, with $V_s \approx \omega^2$: if $V_G = \sqrt{V_m \omega^2}$ and
$V_m = m V_E$, then $\omega = V_G / \sqrt{m V_E}$. The algebra is proved in
`lean/CategoricalQuantGen/Heritability.lean` (`analyticalFitSD_eq`). The width is
therefore exactly the one that would hold the population at the target $h^2 V_P$ if the
Gaussian approximation were right, which makes it a direct test of that approximation.
The paper itself does not use it: it draws $\omega$ at random for each population.

## Equilibrium across the paper's parameter space

We draw 24 parameter sets from the paper's priors [@Pagel2025, Table 1]: phenotypic
variance $V_P$ exponential with mean 0.018 above 0.01 and at most 0.09, heritability
Weibull with shape 1.6 and scale 0.4, mutation scalar gamma with shape 1.1 and scale
0.004, and fitness width uniform on $(0, 10)$. Each population has 1000 individuals and
100 loci with mutation rate $10^{-4}$, as in the paper, and runs for 10,000 generations;
we average the genetic variance and the number of survivors over the last 1000.

```{julia}
function draw_params(rng)
    VP = 0.01 + rand(rng, Exponential(0.018))
    while VP > 0.09; VP = 0.01 + rand(rng, Exponential(0.018)); end
    h2 = rand(rng, Weibull(1.6, 0.4))
    while !(0.01 <= h2 <= 0.99); h2 = rand(rng, Weibull(1.6, 0.4)); end
    (; VP, h2, m = rand(rng, Gamma(1.1, 0.004)), ω = rand(rng, Uniform(0, 10)))
end

function equilibrium(θ; L = 100, gens = 10_000, seed)
    p = Params(PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = L, NoGenerations = gens,
               PhenotypeVar = θ.VP, Heritability = θ.h2, MutationScalar = θ.m,
               MutationRatePerGamete = 1e-4, RecombPoissonMean = 3.0, InitFitnessSD = θ.ω)
    o = simulate(p; seed)
    o.extinct && return nothing
    last = o.gen .>= gens - 1000
    (; p, VG = mean(o.geno_var[last]), ns = mean(o.nsurv[last]))
end

draws = [draw_params(Xoshiro(k)) for k in 1:24]
eq = Vector{Any}(undef, length(draws))
Threads.@threads for k in eachindex(draws)
    eq[k] = equilibrium(draws[k]; seed = k)
end
eq = filter(!isnothing, eq)
length(eq)
```

The two approximations, written for a `Params` value. For $N_e$ we use the number of
survivors: each of the $2N$ gametes of the next generation comes from a survivor chosen
at random, so the number a survivor contributes is binomial with variance
$V_k = 2N (n_s - 1)/n_s^2$ when $n_s$ individuals survive, and
$N_e = 4N/(V_k + 2)$ [@FalconerMackay1996]. This is how the paper's results table
computes it.

```{julia}
gaussian(p) = sqrt(muteVar(p) * (initFitSD(p)^2 + envVar(p)))

function house_of_cards(p, ns)
    N, n, μ = p.PopSize, p.NoQTL, p.MutationRatePerGamete
    Vs = initFitSD(p)^2 + envVar(p)
    α2 = muteVar(p) / (2n * μ)            # variance of one mutation's effect
    Vk = 2N * (ns - 1) / ns^2              # variance in gametes contributed per survivor
    Ne = 4N / (Vk + 2)
    4n * μ * Vs / (1 + Vs / (Ne * α2))
end

shc = [house_of_cards(r.p, r.ns) for r in eq]
gau = [gaussian(r.p) for r in eq]
sim = [r.VG for r in eq]
@printf("simulated / house of cards: median %.2f (range %.2f–%.2f)\n",
        median(sim ./ shc), extrema(sim ./ shc)...)
@printf("simulated / Gaussian:       median %.2f (range %.2f–%.2f)\n",
        median(sim ./ gau), extrema(sim ./ gau)...)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-balance
#| fig-cap: "Equilibrium genetic variance of 24 simulated populations against the two approximations (the line is equality). The stochastic house of cards tracks the simulations across nearly three orders of magnitude; the Gaussian approximation scatters widely, missing by up to a factor of about five in either direction."
fig = Figure(size = (820, 380))
for (k, (pred, name)) in enumerate(((shc, "stochastic house of cards"), (gau, "Gaussian (Lande)")))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, k], xscale = log10, yscale = log10, title = name,
              xlabel = "predicted V_G", ylabel = "simulated V_G")
    lo, hi = extrema(vcat(pred, sim))
    lines!(ax, [lo / 2, 2hi], [lo / 2, 2hi], color = :gray, linestyle = :dash)
    scatter!(ax, pred, sim, color = :teal)
end
fig
```

The house-of-cards regime is the relevant one here because mutation is rare: with 100
loci and a rate of $10^{-4}$ there is only about one new mutation per hundred gametes,
each with an effect large compared with the standing variation at its locus. One
consequence is that the heritability in `Params` is not the heritability the population
ends up with. It only sets the environmental variance, $V_E = (1-h^2)V_P$; the genetic
variance is whatever mutation, selection and drift balance at.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-heritability
#| fig-cap: "Realised heritability V_G/(V_G + V_E) at equilibrium against the nominal heritability that set the environmental variance."
fig = Figure(size = (420, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "nominal h²", ylabel = "realised h²", limits = (0, 1, 0, 1))
lines!(ax, [0, 1], [0, 1], color = :gray, linestyle = :dash)
scatter!(ax, [r.p.Heritability for r in eq],
         [r.VG / (r.VG + envVar(r.p)) for r in eq], color = :crimson)
fig
```

## More loci, more variance

The paper simulated 100, 500, 1000 and 5000 loci. With the mutational input held fixed,
more loci means more frequent mutations of smaller effect, which selection removes less
efficiently, so the house of cards predicts more variance; the Gaussian approximation
does not depend on the number of loci at all. Here one parameter set is run with 10 to
1000 loci.

```{julia}
θ = (VP = 0.02, h2 = 0.4, m = 0.004, ω = 2.0)
Ls = [10, 30, 100, 300, 1000]
byL = Vector{Any}(undef, length(Ls))
Threads.@threads for k in eachindex(Ls)
    byL[k] = equilibrium(θ; L = Ls[k], seed = 100 + k)
end
for (L, r) in zip(Ls, byL)
    @printf("NoQTL = %4d:  simulated %.4f   house of cards %.4f   Gaussian %.4f\n",
            L, r.VG, house_of_cards(r.p, r.ns), gaussian(r.p))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-loci
#| fig-cap: "Equilibrium genetic variance against the number of loci for one parameter set (points), with the house-of-cards prediction (solid) and the Gaussian prediction, which does not depend on the number of loci (dashed)."
fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xscale = log10, xlabel = "number of loci", ylabel = "equilibrium V_G")
lines!(ax, Ls, [house_of_cards(r.p, r.ns) for r in byL], color = :teal, label = "house of cards")
hlines!(ax, [gaussian(byL[1].p)], color = :gray, linestyle = :dash, label = "Gaussian")
scatter!(ax, Ls, [r.VG for r in byL], color = :crimson, label = "simulated")
axislegend(ax, position = :lt)
fig
```

The equilibrium variance grows with the number of loci, as the house of cards predicts,
while the Gaussian approximation misses the trend entirely. In these single runs the
house of cards overestimates the level by about 30% at 100 loci and above. The
[replication vignette](../09_replicating_pagel_2025/09_replicating_pagel_2025.qmd)
makes the same comparison for the paper's own parameter sets.
